title: Monitored Safety-Driver Fallback Pattern
description: A pattern for automated driving systems in which the human-oversight fallback is actively monitored for engagement (not merely required by policy), automatic emergency braking remains enabled throughout autonomous operation, and disengagement events are logged and reviewed.
problem: A nominal 'human in the loop' safety requirement provides no real protection if driver attention is not actually monitored and enforced, and if the system's own emergency-braking safeguards are disabled or under-engineered to allow smoother autonomous operation.
solution: Actively monitor driver engagement (e.g. attention/gaze tracking) during autonomous or driver-assist operation, escalate or restrict system use after repeated disengagement, keep automatic emergency braking enabled at all times, and log every disengagement and near-miss event for periodic safety review.
applicability: Any automated driving or driver-assist system operating on public roads, from supervised test vehicles to consumer driver-assist features.
consequences: Engagement monitoring adds sensor and processing cost and can itself be circumvented by a sufficiently motivated driver; logging disengagement events at fleet scale requires a review process with enough staffing to act on the data, not just collect it.

relationships.reason: Active engagement monitoring is a concrete mechanism satisfying the human-oversight requirement.
Keeping emergency braking enabled throughout autonomous operation addresses this control's accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity requirement.
The pattern's output is a documented safety case covering the oversight fallback.
